newsitem.title: USA: Record labels sees Christmas in not-so-merry year.
newsitem.headline: Record labels sees Christmas in not-so-merry year.

text.p: It's nearly the holiday shopping season, but the $12 billion record industry has been trimming more staff than Christmas trees lately and few executives see a major rebound from sluggish sales soon.

"I think that because it's been such a disappointing first half of the year, record labels are holding down expectations for Christmas," said Hilary Rosen, president, chief operating officer of Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), a trade group based in Washington D.C..
The Christmas quarter accounts for around 40 percent of the industry's annual sales and the industry has begun to see a slight pickup in sales since late September.

"There's a lot of hot products coming out. The potential is there, but it's a real transition year and anybody projecting more than a 1 to 2 percent increase in unit sales in the U.S. is being optimisic," Rosen said.

Sweeping record store closings and bankruptcies as well as cutbacks at major labels, including about 100 layoffs at various labels within Time Warner Inc.'s Warner Music division and 400 at PolyGram NV underscore the market's sluggishness.

But all is not doom and gloom for an industry that in the past two years has plateaued at somewhat lofty levels after several years of soaring sales, fuelled in part by consumers replacing vinyl albums with compact discs.

"This is a good business. It will remain a good business. Growth is flat but flat at very good levels," said a spokesman for Warner Music Group, the market share leader in the domestic record industry.

Hartsdale, N.Y.-based Soundscan, a music marketing research firm, said U.S. album sales were up 2.1 percent in the first nine months of 1996 to 412 million units. But that's down from 474 million in the same period two years ago.
Total album sales for all of 1995 rose by just over one million to 616 million units.

Nevertheless, the music arms of the world's major entertainment conglomerates, like Time Warner and Sony, are still cash cows for these companies and typically more profitable than their glamorous film counterparts.

"It's been a difficult environment, but the record business is doing better than Hollywood (film business). Albums are cheap to produce, the industry has a bigger revenue base and operating costs are not quite as large as for film companies," said Harold Vogel, analyst with Cowen & Co.

Sony, for instance, cited music as its saving grace in the second quarter. Operating income for its entertainment division rose sharply, helped by its music group and a weaker Japanese yen, while its pictures' operating income was flat.
In that quarter, Sony's music sales totalled $1.26 billion, while the pictures group sales were $748.5 million.
"Profitability is relatively constant for these labels," said Rosen, but noted many labels are now cutting costs after expanding rapidly a few years ago to match surging sales.

Distribution arms of the six major labels, which include Seagram Co Ltd.'s MCA Music, Time Warner Inc.'s Warner Bros, Sony Corp.'s Sony Music, Polygram, Bertelsmann Ag's BMG and EMI Group Plc have experienced album returns due to record store bankruptcies.
But many feel the retailing shakeout is nearing an end.

"Store closings have been a cloud over the business and will probably continue into 1997, but we're getting to a point where retail will once again be a profitable business for all," said Henry Droz, who heads distribution for MCA Music, which through acquisitions has been climbing in market share.

New releases by the late Tupac Shakur, the bands Bush and Counting Crows, and others should push MCA's sales up sharply. "Sales in October were up over 50 percent and we see November as potentially our biggest month in history," Droz said.
Rosen said the RIAA was hopeful the industry will see a rebound at the the retail level, beginning next year.

"The retail orders have been relatively cautious, but the good news is returns (to suppliers) are likely to be down. When retail inventories are tighter, it's easier for record companies to keep costs down," Rosen said.
Despite the sluggishness, the industry remains bullish and many are releasing new albums for the upcoming holiday season.

"Music is still compelling to consumers. While we're going through a corrective transition process, given the difficulty on some of our retail accounts, I'm still bullish about music and the importance of music to consumers," said Pete Jones, president of BMG's distribution division, which is soon releasing a Whitney Houston album for the holidays.
Label executives say there is no exact science to the business, which fluctuates according to the public's whim.
The competition to find the next major breakthrough artist like Michael Jackson or Madonna, is fiercer than ever.
"I think the biggest challenge to the entire business is in getting traffic stoppers. You want someone who is going to motivate people to come into a store," said Bob Merlis, a spokesman at Warner.
Warner this year struck gold with multi-million unit selling sensation Alanis Morissette, and is selling a new Van Halen album and the Evita soundtrack in this holiday season.
All the labels have several albums set to be released this quarter and have been spending heavily on promotions.

"The price of one title in our top 30 retail accounts is going up every year by hundreds of thousands of dollars because of the increased cost of media the accounts have to buy and because the acounts' growing appetite for advertising and in-store promotions," said Jones of BMG.
